entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A standard or principle used to judge, choose or decide something.
entries.usage: Common in work, education, law and research: *selection / eligibility criteria*, *meet the criteria*, *the main criterion*. Many natives now use *criteria* as a singular in speech, but careful writers keep *one criterion, two criteria*. It usually refers to formal, stated standards rather than personal taste.
entries.pattern: meet / fit the criteria (for something); the main / only criterion; selection / eligibility criteria
examples: To get the scholarship, students must meet three **criteria**: good grades, community service and financial need.
Price was our only **criterion** when we picked a hotel; we just needed somewhere to sleep.
The judges score each dish on four **criteria**, including taste and presentation.

drill.sentence: Your house doesn't meet the {{criteria}} for the energy rebate because it was built after 2010.
drill.hint: the rules for who qualifies (not *requirements*, *conditions* or *standards*)

mistake.wrong: The most important criteria is cost.
mistake.right: The most important criterion is cost.
mistake.why: *Criteria* is the plural; for one standard, use *criterion*.

entries.related: *standard* — a level of quality; *requirement* — something you must have or do; *yardstick* — something used to measure or compare.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Not certain or final, because it may still change; or done without confidence, in a hesitant way.
entries.usage: Very common in planning: *a tentative date / plan / agreement / schedule*, *tentatively scheduled for* Friday. In emails and calendars, *tentative* tells others that a time is not fixed yet. About actions it means shy or uncertain: *a tentative smile*, *tentative first steps*.
entries.pattern: a tentative date / plan / agreement; a tentative smile / step; tentatively scheduled / planned
examples: We've set a **tentative** date for the wedding, but it depends on the venue.
The baby took a few **tentative** steps toward the coffee table.
The union and the airline have reached a **tentative** agreement, but members still have to vote on it.

drill.sentence: The puppy gave the cat a {{tentative}} sniff, then jumped back when it hissed.
drill.hint: done without confidence, ready to pull back (not *cautious*, *careful*, *hesitant*, *nervous* or *curious*)

entries.related: *provisional* — formal, temporary until confirmed; *hesitant* — slow to act because unsure; *definite* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The amount of work that a person or group has to do in a particular period.
entries.usage: Common at work, in schools and in healthcare: *a heavy / light / manageable workload*, *reduce / increase someone's workload*, *spread the workload*. It is one word and refers to the whole amount, so natives describe it as *heavy* or *light*. With *a lot of*, they simply say *work*.
entries.pattern: a heavy / light / manageable workload; reduce / increase / spread the workload
examples: Nurses on the night shift have a much heavier **workload** since two colleagues left.
My **workload** is lighter in July, so that's when I take vacation.
Most students find the **workload** in their first year of college much heavier than in high school.

drill.sentence: My sister had to drop a class because her {{workload}} at the restaurant doubled over the holidays.
drill.hint: amount of tasks to handle (not *hours*, *shifts* or *schedule*)

mistake.wrong: I have a lot of workload this week.
mistake.right: I have a heavy workload this week.
mistake.why: *Workload* is the total amount, so it is *heavy* or *light*; with *a lot of*, natives say *a lot of work*.

entries.related: *caseload* — the number of cases a doctor, lawyer or social worker handles; *backlog* — work that has piled up; *workflow* — the order in which work is done.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A problem or event that delays progress or makes a situation worse than it was before.
entries.usage: Common in news, sports, health and business: *a major / minor / temporary setback*, *suffer / face / overcome a setback*, *a setback for* a team or plan. It suggests that progress can continue later, so it sounds less final than *failure*. The noun is one word; the verb is *set back* (*the injury set him back a month*).
entries.pattern: a major / minor / temporary setback; suffer / face / overcome a setback; a setback for someone
examples: Losing their star player to injury was a major **setback** for the team.
The bakery suffered a **setback** when its oven broke during the holiday rush.
Recovery after surgery isn't a straight line; a few **setbacks** are normal.

drill.sentence: We were almost done renovating the kitchen when a burst pipe caused a big {{setback}}.
drill.hint: something that pushed progress back (not *delay*, *problem* or *mess*)

entries.related: *hiccup* — informal, a small, short problem; *obstacle* — something in the way; *breakthrough* — the opposite, a sudden step forward.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To decide which things are most important and deal with them first, or to treat something as more important than other things.
entries.usage: Very common at work and in health or self-help advice: *prioritize tasks / your health / sleep / safety*, *prioritize A over B*, *learn to prioritize*. It can be used without an object (*you need to prioritize*). American spelling is *-ize*; the noun is *priority* (*make something a priority*).
entries.pattern: prioritize tasks / your health / safety; prioritize A over B
examples: With three deadlines this week, I have to **prioritize** and let the smaller tasks wait.
After my health scare, I started **prioritizing** sleep over late-night TV.
The city says it will **prioritize** fixing roads near schools.

drill.sentence: When you're packing for a short trip, {{prioritize}} the things you can't easily buy at your destination.
drill.hint: put first in order of importance (not *pack*, *bring*, *choose* or *focus on*)

entries.related: *put first* — plainer; *rank* — put in order; *focus on* — give your attention to.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A difference between two things that should be the same, such as numbers, reports or accounts.
entries.usage: Common in finance, law, journalism, healthcare and research: *a discrepancy between A and B*, *a discrepancy in* the numbers, *notice / explain a discrepancy*. It suggests that something may be wrong and needs checking. It is more formal than *difference* or *mismatch*.
entries.pattern: a discrepancy between A and B; a discrepancy in the figures / accounts; notice / explain a discrepancy
examples: I noticed a **discrepancy** between the price on the shelf and the price on my receipt.
Police found **discrepancies** in the two drivers' stories about the accident.
The accountant flagged a $300 **discrepancy** in last month's bank statement.

drill.sentence: There's a {{discrepancy}} between the number of chairs we ordered and the number that arrived.
drill.hint: something that doesn't add up (not *difference*, *mismatch* or *gap*)

entries.related: *inconsistency* — parts that don't agree; *mismatch* — things that don't fit together; *disparity* — a large, often unfair difference.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Something that limits what you can do, such as a lack of time, money or space, or a rule.
entries.usage: Common in business, engineering, planning and academic writing: *time / budget / financial constraints*, *work within constraints*, *a constraint on* growth. It is often plural and sounds neutral and professional, so *due to time constraints* is a polite way to explain why something cannot be done. In design and math, constraints are the fixed conditions a solution must meet.
entries.pattern: time / budget / space constraints; a constraint on something; work within constraints
examples: Due to time **constraints**, we'll skip the Q&A and take questions by email.
Our biggest **constraint** in the new apartment is space; there's no room for a desk.
Budget **constraints** forced the town to cancel this year's fireworks show.

drill.sentence: Working within the {{constraints}} of a tiny kitchen and a fifty-dollar budget, she still made dinner for twelve people.
drill.hint: factors that limit what you can do (not *limits*, *limitations* or *confines*)

entries.related: *limitation* — a weakness or limit, often of a method; *restriction* — a rule that limits; *bottleneck* — one point that slows everything down.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A disadvantage or problem that makes something less attractive or useful.
entries.usage: Very common in reviews, conversation and business writing: *the main / only / biggest drawback*, *the drawback of / to* something, *benefits and drawbacks*. It is softer than *problem*: the thing is usually still good overall. It is written as one word.
entries.pattern: the main / only / biggest drawback (of / to something); benefits and drawbacks
examples: The apartment is perfect; the only **drawback** is the lack of parking.
One **drawback** of working from home is that you never really leave the office.
Electric cars are cheap to run, but the main **drawback** is charging time on long road trips.

drill.sentence: I love my new phone; its one real {{drawback}} is the battery, which dies by dinnertime.
drill.hint: thing that makes it less good (not *downside*, *flaw*, *weakness*, *issue* or *problem*)

entries.related: *downside* — informal, very common in speech; *disadvantage* — more formal and general; *catch* — a hidden drawback (*what's the catch?*).

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Based on good reasoning or judgment, and therefore sensible and reliable.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, business and law: *sound advice*, *sound judgment*, *a sound investment*, *financially sound*, *scientifically sound*. It is positive and slightly formal, and it describes ideas, decisions, methods and finances rather than people. *Safe and sound* (unharmed) and *of sound mind* (mentally healthy, a legal phrase) use related senses.
entries.pattern: sound advice / judgment / reasoning / investment; financially / scientifically sound
examples: My grandfather gave me some **sound** advice: never borrow money to buy something you don't need.
Before lending money, the bank checks that the business is financially **sound**.
The idea is interesting, but the reasoning behind it isn't very **sound**.

drill.sentence: Buying a small condo near the university turned out to be a {{sound}} investment; rents there keep going up.
drill.hint: based on good judgment (not *good*, *smart*, *wise*, *safe* or *solid*)

entries.related: *solid* — informal, dependable; *valid* — logically correct, about arguments; *unsound* — the opposite (*unsound reasoning*).

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Limited to one person, group or organization and not shared with others.
entries.usage: Common in business, media and shopping: *exclusive rights / access / deals*, *exclusive to* members or one store, *an exclusive interview*. It also means expensive and open only to a few people (*an exclusive club*). *Mutually exclusive* means two things cannot both be true or happen at the same time.
entries.pattern: exclusive to someone / something; exclusive rights / access / deal / interview; mutually exclusive
examples: This color is **exclusive** to our website; you won't find it in any of our stores.
The network paid billions for **exclusive** rights to broadcast the Olympics.
Are you and Mark **exclusive** now, or are you still seeing other people?

drill.sentence: Members get {{exclusive}} access to the pool before 8 a.m., when it's closed to everyone else.
drill.hint: only for them, not shared (not *special*, *private*, *early* or *priority*)

entries.related: *sole* — only (*the sole owner*); *private* — not open to the public; *inclusive* — the opposite, including everyone.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To stop something harmful, such as a fire, disease, problem or strong emotion, from spreading or getting worse.
entries.usage: Common in news, emergency and medical language: *contain a fire / an outbreak / the spread / the damage*. American wildfire reports give a percentage: *the fire is 60 percent contained*. For emotions it usually appears with *can't* or *barely* (*she could barely contain her excitement*).
entries.pattern: contain a fire / an outbreak / the spread / the damage; can't / barely contain your excitement / anger
examples: By Sunday night, firefighters had **contained** most of the wildfire.
Health officials moved quickly to **contain** the outbreak at the summer camp.
After the bad call, the coach could barely **contain** his anger and had to walk away from the referee.

drill.sentence: We put towels around the leaking dishwasher to {{contain}} the water until the plumber arrived.
drill.hint: hold back so it can't spread (not *stop*, *catch* or *absorb*)

entries.related: *control* — keep in order, more general; *curb* — limit something bad; *rein in* — informal, get under control.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To start or set up an organization, system or relationship that is meant to last; or to prove or show that something is true.
entries.usage: Common in business, law, history and news: *establish a company / rules / a routine / contact* and *establish that…* or *establish the cause / the facts*. Both senses sound more formal and permanent than *set up* or *find out*. The adjective *established* means accepted and respected (*an established writer*).
entries.pattern: establish a company / system / routine / relationship; establish that … / the cause / the facts
examples: The family **established** the restaurant in 1952, and the grandchildren still run it today.
Investigators are still trying to **establish** what caused the fire.
It helps to **establish** a bedtime routine when kids are very young.

drill.sentence: The DNA test {{established}} that the two men were brothers who had been separated at birth.
drill.hint: made certain as a fact (not *proved*, *confirmed*, *showed*, *determined* or *revealed*)

entries.related: *set up* — informal, start a business or system; *found* — start an organization; *determine* — formal, find out exactly.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To promise firmly that something will happen or is true, or to make an outcome certain.
entries.usage: Common in business, ads and everyday talk: *guarantee that…*, *guarantee results / delivery / a refund*, *be guaranteed to* + verb. *I guarantee you…* is casual and emphatic. It is very often negative, because few things are certain: *can't guarantee*, *doesn't guarantee success*.
entries.pattern: guarantee that …; guarantee someone something; be guaranteed to + verb; can't guarantee
examples: The store **guarantees** your money back if you're not happy within thirty days.
I **guarantee** you he'll be late; he's never been on time in his life.
A college degree no longer **guarantees** a good job.

drill.sentence: We can't {{guarantee}} you'll get a window seat, but we'll do our best.
drill.hint: give a firm assurance (not *promise* or *ensure*)

mistake.why: English spells it with *gua-*, unlike German *garantieren*; the *u* is silent.

entries.related: *promise* — more personal; *ensure* — make certain, formal; *warranty* — a written guarantee for a product.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To make known something that was secret or unknown, or to show something that was hidden.
entries.usage: Very common in news, entertainment and conversation: *reveal a secret / the truth / the winner*, *reveal that…*, *it was revealed that…*. It sounds more dramatic than *tell* or *show* and suggests that something was hidden before. As a noun, *the big reveal* is the moment a surprise is shown, as on a TV show.
entries.pattern: reveal a secret / the truth / the results; reveal that …; reveal something to someone
examples: In the last chapter, the author finally **reveals** who stole the painting.
A new survey **reveals** that most Americans eat lunch at their desks.
When she took off her hat, she **revealed** a bright pink haircut.

drill.sentence: My grandma kept the recipe secret for fifty years and only {{revealed}} it on her ninetieth birthday.
drill.hint: made it known (not *shared*, *told* or *disclosed*)

entries.related: *disclose* — formal, often legal or financial; *expose* — reveal something bad; *conceal* — the opposite, hide.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The health, safety and happiness of a person or animal; in American English also government money and help for people with little or no income.
entries.usage: The first sense is formal and common in law, schools and animal care: *child welfare*, *animal welfare*, *concern for someone's welfare*. In the US, *be on welfare* is the everyday way to say someone receives government cash or food assistance; official texts usually say *public assistance* or name the program. British English says *on benefits*.
entries.pattern: child / animal welfare; concern for someone's welfare; be on welfare
examples: The shelter takes animal **welfare** seriously: every dog is walked twice a day.
Teachers are required to report any concerns about a child's **welfare**.
After losing her job, she was on **welfare** for a few months while she trained as a nurse.

drill.sentence: The camp counselors are responsible for the {{welfare}} of forty kids for two whole weeks.
drill.hint: how they are doing, body and mind (not *safety*, *well-being* or *care*)

entries.related: *well-being* — more common for health and happiness; *benefits* — government payments; *Social Security* — in the US, mainly the federal retirement program.

entries.label: conjunction
entries.meaning: Used to compare two facts and show how they are different, like *while on the other hand*.
entries.usage: Common in writing and careful speech to contrast two clauses, usually after a comma, or at the start (*Whereas A, B*). In casual talk *while* or *but* is more natural. Unlike German *während*, it shows only contrast, never two things happening at the same time.
entries.pattern: clause, whereas + contrasting clause; Whereas A, B
examples: My brother loves big cities, **whereas** I'd rather live somewhere quiet.
Some people need eight hours of sleep, **whereas** others feel fine after six.
The old phone plan charged a flat fee, **whereas** the new one charges by the minute.

drill.sentence: Cats tend to be fine on their own, {{whereas}} dogs need company most of the day.
drill.hint: introducing a contrast, a bit formal (not *while* or *but*)

mistake.wrong: Whereas I was cooking, the phone rang.
mistake.right: While I was cooking, the phone rang.
mistake.why: *Whereas* only shows contrast; for two things happening at the same time, use *while*.

entries.related: *while* — same contrast, more common in speech, also used for time; *whilst* — British, formal; *on the other hand* — starts a new sentence.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Very strong, extreme or concentrated, in feeling, amount or activity.
entries.usage: Very common for feelings, experiences, heat, light and competition: *intense pain / pressure / heat / competition / debate*. About a person it means very serious and emotional, sometimes too much (*he's a bit intense*). Do not confuse it with *intensive*, which means packing a lot into a short time (*intensive care*, *an intensive course*).
entries.pattern: intense pain / heat / pressure / competition / debate; a bit / pretty intense
examples: The heat in Death Valley was so **intense** that we barely left the car.
There's **intense** competition for summer internships at big law firms.
Our first date was a little **intense**; he asked about my five-year plan.

drill.sentence: The final minutes of the game were so {{intense}} that half the crowd was on its feet.
drill.hint: extremely strong in feeling (not *tense*, *exciting*, *thrilling* or *dramatic*)

mistake.wrong: The pain was so intensive that I couldn't sleep.
mistake.right: The pain was so intense that I couldn't sleep.
mistake.why: Strong pain, feelings, heat or colors are *intense*; *intensive* means packing a lot of work into a short time (*intensive care*, *an intensive course*), and German *intensiv* covers both.

entries.related: *intensive* — concentrated, thorough; *fierce* — strong and aggressive, about competition or weather; *mild* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To watch, check or measure something regularly over a period of time to see how it changes.
entries.usage: Common in health, work, science and news: *monitor someone's blood pressure / progress / spending*, *monitor the situation*. It suggests regular, careful observation, often with equipment. *Closely* is a very frequent partner (*we're monitoring it closely*).
entries.pattern: monitor + progress / blood pressure / the situation / spending; closely monitor
examples: Nurses **monitored** her heart rate all night after the surgery.
Forecasters are closely **monitoring** a storm moving up the coast.
The app helps parents **monitor** how much time their kids spend online.

drill.sentence: If you have diabetes, you'll need to {{monitor}} your blood sugar several times a day.
drill.hint: watch regularly over time (not *check*, *test*, *measure* or *track*)

entries.related: *track* — follow over time, often data or packages; *supervise* — watch people to make sure they act correctly; *keep an eye on* — informal.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Permission or agreement to do something, especially when it is given clearly and freely.
entries.usage: Common in medicine, law, schools and privacy settings: *give / get / withdraw consent*, *without someone's consent*, *written / parental consent*, *informed consent*. It is more formal than *permission* and stresses the person's right to say no. The verb *consent to* is formal (*she consented to the search*).
entries.pattern: give / obtain / withdraw consent; without someone's consent; parental / written consent
examples: Students under eighteen need a parent's written **consent** to go on the field trip.
The surgeon explained the risks before asking for her **consent**.
Don't post photos of other people's kids without their parents' **consent**.

drill.sentence: The neighbors cut down the big oak on our property line without our {{consent}}.
drill.hint: formal agreement that it was okay (not *permission*, *knowledge* or *approval*)

entries.related: *permission* — more general and everyday; *approval* — official acceptance; *assent* — formal, agreement.

mistake.wrong: After a long meeting, we finally reached a consent.
mistake.right: After a long meeting, we finally reached a consensus.
mistake.why: German *Konsens* is *consensus* (general agreement) in English; *consent* means permission.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Very new and different, and affecting the most basic parts of something, so that a change is extreme and far-reaching.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and history: *radical change / reform / idea / shift*, *a radical departure from*, *a radical overhaul*. It can sound positive (bold) or negative (too extreme), depending on the speaker. About people's views it means extreme, and then it is often a critical label.
entries.pattern: radical change / reform / shift / idea; a radical departure from something; a radical overhaul
examples: Moving to a farm after twenty years in Manhattan was a **radical** change for our family.
The architect's design was a **radical** departure from the town's old brick buildings.
Some doctors say back pain needs a **radical** new approach: less surgery and more exercise.

drill.sentence: Cutting out sugar completely was a pretty {{radical}} step, but my energy levels improved within a week.
drill.hint: changing things at the most basic level (not *drastic*, *big*, *bold* or *extreme*)

entries.related: *drastic* — extreme and sudden, often about measures; *fundamental* — about the basic nature of something; *gradual* — the opposite, slow.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Full of energy, new ideas and enthusiasm; also, constantly changing and developing.
entries.usage: Very common in job ads, business and reviews: *a dynamic leader / team / city / speaker*, *a dynamic market*. In job ads it is a cliché (*a dynamic, fast-paced environment*), so it can sound empty. As a noun, *a dynamic* is the way people in a group interact (*the family dynamic*).
entries.pattern: a dynamic leader / team / city / speaker; a dynamic market / situation
examples: She's a **dynamic** speaker who can keep a room of teenagers listening for an hour.
Austin has become one of the most **dynamic** cities in the country, with new businesses opening every week.
In such a **dynamic** market, flight prices can change several times a day.

drill.sentence: The new principal is young and {{dynamic}}, and she's already started a robotics club and a school garden.
drill.hint: full of energy and new ideas (not *energetic*, *ambitious*, *creative* or *driven*)

entries.related: *energetic* — full of physical energy; *vibrant* — lively and exciting, often about places; *static* — the opposite, not changing.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Causing worry; somewhat worrying.
entries.usage: Very common in American speech, news and medicine: *That's concerning*, *a concerning trend*, *the results are concerning*, *deeply concerning*. It sounds calm and measured, a softer way to say that something is worrying. Many British speakers still prefer *worrying*; as a preposition, *concerning* means *about* (*questions concerning the schedule*).
entries.pattern: That's concerning; a concerning trend / sign / number; deeply concerning
examples: He hasn't answered his phone in two days, which is a little **concerning**.
Doctors say the rise in sports injuries among young kids is **concerning**.
That grinding noise the car is making is **concerning**; I'd get it checked before the trip.

drill.sentence: The doctor said the spot on the X-ray probably wasn't serious, but it was {{concerning}} enough to check again in six months.
drill.hint: causing some worry (not *worrying*, *worrisome* or *suspicious*)

entries.related: *worrying* — same meaning, more common in British English; *worrisome* — American, a bit more formal; *alarming* — much stronger.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Fairness, especially in how people are treated or paid; in finance, the value of shares in a company, or the part of a property's value that you own after debts.
entries.usage: In the fairness sense it is formal and common in workplace, education and health policy (*pay equity*, *health equity*). In finance it means ownership: *equity in a company*, *private equity*, and in the US *home equity*, the share of your home's value you own outright. In both senses it is more technical than *fairness* or *ownership*.
entries.pattern: equity in a company / home; home equity; private equity; pay / health equity
examples: After ten years of mortgage payments, we have quite a bit of **equity** in our house.
Instead of a high salary, the startup offered me **equity** in the company.
A pay **equity** review found that three nurses were earning less than colleagues with the same experience.

drill.sentence: They borrowed against the {{equity}} in their home to pay for their daughter's college tuition.
drill.hint: share of the property's value they own outright (not *value*)

entries.related: *equality* — being equal in rights or status; *fairness* — the everyday word; *stock* / *shares* — units of ownership in a company.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To formally hand in a document, proposal, application or piece of work so that someone can judge or approve it.
entries.usage: Very common at work, at school and online: *submit an application / a proposal / a claim / homework*, *submit something to* someone *by* a date. It is more formal than *hand in*, *turn in* or *send in*, and online forms usually end with a *Submit* button. A different sense is to give in to power (*submit to authority*).
entries.pattern: submit an application / a proposal / a claim / a request (to someone) (by a date)
examples: All applications must be **submitted** online by March 1.
After the storm, we **submitted** a claim to our insurance company for the roof damage.
Residents can **submit** ideas for the new park through the city's website.

drill.sentence: My son finished his science project at 11:58 p.m. and {{submitted}} it two minutes before the deadline.
drill.hint: officially sent in (not *uploaded*, *turned in* or *handed in*)

entries.related: *hand in* / *turn in* — informal, especially for schoolwork; *file* — submit an official document (*file a complaint*); *withdraw* — take back.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To argue or say that a fact, claim or decision is not true, correct or fair.
entries.usage: Common in news, law, finance and sports: *dispute a claim / a charge / the results / a call*, *dispute that…*, *no one disputes that…*. You can *dispute a charge* on your credit card to ask the bank to reverse it. It is more formal than *argue with* or *challenge*.
entries.pattern: dispute a claim / charge / decision / fact; dispute that …; nobody disputes that …
examples: I **disputed** the charge on my credit card, and the bank refunded it within a week.
The coach **disputed** the referee's call, but the goal still counted.
Nobody **disputes** that the bridge needs repairs; the question is who pays.

drill.sentence: The landlord kept our deposit, but we {{disputed}} his claim that we'd damaged the floors.
drill.hint: argued it was not true (not *challenged*, *denied*, *contested* or *fought*)

entries.related: *challenge* — question whether something is right; *contest* — formally dispute, often in law; *deny* — say something is not true.

entries.label: adjective / noun
entries.meaning: Accepted by or typical of most people, and therefore common or ordinary rather than unusual or extreme.
entries.usage: Common in media, culture, business and politics: *mainstream media / culture / music / medicine*, *go mainstream*, *enter the mainstream*. Among fans of niche culture it can sound slightly negative (*they've gone mainstream*). As a noun it means the ideas, styles or people most widely accepted (*outside the mainstream*).
entries.pattern: mainstream culture / media / music / medicine; go mainstream; (enter / outside) the mainstream
examples: Tattoos used to seem rebellious, but now they're completely **mainstream**.
Sushi went from a rare treat to a **mainstream** food in the U.S. in just a few decades.
The band played small clubs for years before it finally broke into the **mainstream**.

drill.sentence: Electric bikes used to be rare, but they've become totally {{mainstream}}; half my neighbors ride one.
drill.hint: accepted and used by most people (not *popular*, *normal*, *common* or *commonplace*)

entries.related: *conventional* — following accepted ways; *niche* — appealing to a small, special group; *fringe* — at the extreme edge.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A public disagreement or argument about something, often lasting a long time and involving strong feelings.
entries.usage: Very common in news and conversation: *spark / cause / stir up controversy*, *a controversy over / about* something, *surrounded by controversy*. It is uncountable for the general situation and countable for a specific case (*a new controversy*). Americans stress the first syllable, KAHN-truh-vur-see.
entries.pattern: spark / cause / stir up controversy; a controversy over / about something; surrounded by controversy
examples: The referee's decision in the final minute caused huge **controversy** among fans.
The plan to cut down the old oak trees in the park sparked **controversy** in town.
Despite all the **controversy** over its ending, the show was renewed for a second season.

drill.sentence: The new rule banning phones during school lunch has stirred up a lot of {{controversy}} among parents.
drill.hint: strong public disagreement between two sides (not *debate*, *criticism*, *drama* or *anger*)

entries.related: *debate* — a discussion of different views, less emotional; *scandal* — a case of shocking wrongdoing; *controversial* — the adjective.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A full range of different opinions, types, qualities or situations, from one extreme to the other.
entries.usage: Common in news, psychology and discussion: *a wide / broad spectrum of*, *across the spectrum*, *at the other end of the spectrum*, and *on the spectrum*, which usually refers to autism. The figurative sense comes from the range of colors in light. The plural is *spectrums* or, more formally, *spectra*.
entries.pattern: a wide / broad spectrum of something; across the spectrum; at the other / opposite end of the spectrum
examples: The evening class attracts a wide **spectrum** of students, from teenagers to retirees.
At the other end of the **spectrum**, some hotels in the city charge $1,000 a night.
Reactions to the new menu covered the whole **spectrum**, from love to complete disgust.

drill.sentence: Our book club has a broad {{spectrum}} of tastes: some members love thrillers, others only read poetry.
drill.hint: full span from one extreme to the other (not *range*, *mix* or *variety*)

entries.related: *range* — more general and common; *continuum* — formal, a smooth scale with no clear breaks; *gamut* — the whole range (*run the gamut*).

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: Only, and not involving anyone or anything else; for one person, group or purpose.
entries.usage: Common in writing, ads and news: *almost / mostly exclusively*, *available exclusively at / on*, *focus exclusively on*. It is stronger and more formal than *only* and stresses that there are no exceptions. *Mostly, but not exclusively,* means mainly but not only.
entries.pattern: (almost) exclusively + noun / verb; available exclusively at / on; focus exclusively on
examples: The new sneakers are available **exclusively** on the company's website.
For two weeks, the baby ate almost **exclusively** mashed bananas.
The clinic works **exclusively** with children under twelve.

drill.sentence: This beach is reserved {{exclusively}} for hotel guests, so we had to find another spot.
drill.hint: for nobody else (not *only*, *solely* or *strictly*)

entries.related: *solely* — formal, only; *entirely* — completely; *primarily* — mainly, but not only.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Most powerful, important, noticeable or common in a group or situation.
entries.usage: Common in business, sports, science and news: *a dominant position / force / player / team*, *the dominant culture*, *your dominant hand*. In sports it is high praise (*a dominant performance*). In biology, a *dominant gene* is the one that shows its effect when paired with a recessive one.
entries.pattern: a dominant player / team / force / position; dominant in a market; your dominant hand
examples: The team was **dominant** all season and lost only two games.
Online stores have become the **dominant** way Americans buy books.
She broke her right wrist, which is a problem because that's her **dominant** hand.

drill.sentence: Red is the {{dominant}} color in the living room, so we picked gray cushions to calm it down.
drill.hint: standing out most, over all others (not *main*, *primary*, *predominant* or *strongest*)

entries.related: *predominant* — most common or noticeable, more formal; *leading* — first or best; *dominate* — the verb.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Lasting for a long time, or happening again and again, and difficult to cure or solve.
entries.usage: Mainly medical (*chronic pain / illness / fatigue / disease*), the opposite of *acute*, which means sudden and short. It is also used for long-lasting problems and habits: *a chronic shortage*, *chronic lack of sleep*, *a chronic complainer*. It means long-lasting, not severe: a chronic condition can be mild, and an acute one very serious.
entries.pattern: chronic pain / illness / fatigue / disease; a chronic shortage of something; a chronic liar / complainer
examples: My mom has lived with **chronic** back pain since a car accident in her thirties.
The town has a **chronic** shortage of affordable housing.
He's a **chronic** complainer; nothing is ever good enough for him.

drill.sentence: Years of working night shifts left him with {{chronic}} insomnia that no sleeping pill could fix.
drill.hint: long-term and hard to cure (not *severe*, *persistent* or *terrible*)

entries.related: *acute* — sudden and short, the medical opposite; *persistent* — continuing; *habitual* — done as a habit (*a habitual liar*).

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To keep something safe from harm, loss or change, so that it stays in its original or good state.
entries.usage: Common in history, nature, food, law and news: *preserve a building / tradition / habitat / evidence*, *well-preserved*, *preserve food* by drying, salting or canning. It suggests keeping something valuable for the future. Watch the false friend: English *preservative* is a chemical that keeps food fresh, not German *Präservativ* (a condom).
entries.pattern: preserve a building / tradition / habitat / food / evidence; well-preserved
examples: Volunteers are working to **preserve** the old lighthouse for future generations.
My grandmother **preserved** peaches every summer in big glass jars.
The family has worked hard to **preserve** their holiday traditions after moving across the country.

drill.sentence: The mummy was so well {{preserved}} that you could still see the details of its face.
drill.hint: protected from decay over time (not *kept* or *maintained*)

entries.related: *conserve* — protect or use carefully, often energy or nature; *protect* — keep from harm; *preservative* — a chemical that keeps food fresh.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: Almost or very nearly; or in a way that is realistic and useful rather than theoretical.
entries.usage: In conversation the *almost* sense is far more common: *practically everyone*, *practically nothing*, *practically impossible*, *I practically live here*. It often adds a little humor or exaggeration. In the second sense it usually comes in *practically speaking* at the start of a sentence.
entries.pattern: practically + everyone / nothing / impossible / every day; practically speaking
examples: The restaurant was **practically** empty, so we got a table by the window.
My son **practically** lives at his friend's house during the summer.
It sounds great in theory, but **practically** speaking, we don't have the staff.

drill.sentence: It rained {{practically}} every day of our vacation, so we spent most of it in museums.
drill.hint: all but, with a bit of exaggeration (not *almost*, *nearly*, *basically* or *virtually*)

entries.related: *virtually* — very close in meaning, a bit more formal; *basically* — informal; *in practice* — in reality, as opposed to theory.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To continue doing something that has already started, or to go on to the next step or place.
entries.usage: Formal and common in official, legal, business and travel language: *proceed with* a plan, *proceed to* the next step or a place, *proceed to* + verb, *How should we proceed?*. Airport and train announcements use it often (*please proceed to Gate 12*). In casual talk people say *go ahead*, *go on* or *move on*.
entries.pattern: proceed with something; proceed to + place / next step; proceed to + verb
examples: Attention shoppers: the store will be closing shortly. Please **proceed** to the nearest open register.
After the inspection, we decided to **proceed** with buying the house.
The judge allowed the case to **proceed** to trial.

drill.sentence: Once the glue is completely dry, you can {{proceed}} to the next step: sanding the edges.
drill.hint: go forward, in formal instructions (not *move on* or *continue*)

mistake.wrong: The awards ceremony will be proceeded by a short dinner.
mistake.right: The awards ceremony will be preceded by a short dinner.
mistake.why: *Precede* means come before; *proceed* means continue or go forward.

entries.related: *continue* — more neutral; *go ahead* — informal, start or continue; *proceeds* — noun, the money raised from a sale or event.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To bring something back to its earlier good condition, or to bring back something that was lost, such as power, order or trust.
entries.usage: Common in news, home repair, art and tech: *restore power / order / peace / trust*, *restore an old car / a painting*, *restore a phone to factory settings*. After outages, news reports say *power has been restored*. It suggests careful work to return to an original state, not just a quick repair.
entries.pattern: restore power / service / order / trust / confidence; restore something to its original condition
examples: Power was **restored** to most homes about six hours after the storm.
My uncle spent ten years **restoring** a 1965 Mustang in his garage.
It will take time to **restore** trust after a betrayal like that.

drill.sentence: The museum spent two years {{restoring}} the painting, carefully removing centuries of dirt and old varnish.
drill.hint: returning to its original condition (not *cleaning*, *repairing* or *fixing*)

entries.related: *renovate* — repair and improve a building; *repair* — fix something broken; *revive* — bring back to life or popularity.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The careful, continuous watching of people, places or activities, often by police, governments or security systems.
entries.usage: Common in news, law, security and health: *under surveillance*, *video surveillance*, *surveillance cameras / footage*. It often sounds serious or raises privacy concerns. In public health, *disease surveillance* simply means tracking cases.
entries.pattern: under surveillance; surveillance cameras / footage / equipment; video surveillance
examples: Police had the suspect under **surveillance** for weeks before the arrest.
**Surveillance** footage showed a man taking a package from our porch.
The store increased **surveillance** after a string of shoplifting incidents.

drill.sentence: The bank robbers didn't realize that every move they made was being recorded by {{surveillance}} cameras.
drill.hint: used for watching people (not *security*, *hidden* or *video*)

entries.related: *monitoring* — regular checking, more neutral; *spying* — secret watching, negative; *CCTV* — closed-circuit TV, the usual British term for camera surveillance.

entries.label: noun / verb
entries.meaning: A legal contract that lets someone use an apartment, house, car or land for a fixed time in exchange for regular payments.
entries.usage: Very common in American everyday life: *sign / renew / break a lease*, *a one-year lease*, *the lease is up / runs out*. Americans *rent* an apartment under a lease and often *lease* a car (pay monthly, then return it). As a verb, the owner *leases* something *to* you, and you *lease* it *from* them.
entries.pattern: sign / renew / break a lease; a one-year lease; lease a car / an apartment (from someone)
examples: Our **lease** is up in August, so we're starting to look for a bigger place.
If you break your **lease** early, you'll probably lose your security deposit.
Instead of buying a car, my sister **leases** a new one every three years.

drill.sentence: We signed a twelve-month {{lease}}, but the landlord let us move out after ten.
drill.hint: legal deal to rent the apartment (not *contract* or *agreement*)

mistake.wrong: I have a leasing for my car.
mistake.right: I have a lease on my car.
mistake.why: German *Leasing* is the contract; in English the contract is *a lease*, and *leasing* is the activity.

entries.related: *rental agreement* — often shorter or less formal; *sublet* — rent your leased place to someone else; *mortgage* — a loan to buy a home.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: At exactly the same time.
entries.usage: Common in news, instructions and technical or academic writing: *happen / occur / run simultaneously*, *simultaneously + verb*. In casual speech *at the same time* is more natural. Americans usually start it with *sy* (like *sign*), while many British speakers say *sim*.
entries.pattern: happen / occur / run / work simultaneously; simultaneously + verb
examples: The movie was released **simultaneously** in theaters and on streaming.
Both kids started crying **simultaneously** the moment the plane took off.
At the hearing, an interpreter translated every word **simultaneously** into Spanish.

drill.sentence: It's hard to drive and talk on the phone {{simultaneously}}, even with a headset.
drill.hint: both in one moment, said formally (not *at once* or *together*)

entries.related: *at the same time* — the everyday phrase; *concurrently* — formal, used in law and computing; *in sync* — at the same time and coordinated.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Legal responsibility for damage, injury or debt; also, a person or thing that causes problems or puts others at a disadvantage.
entries.usage: The legal sense is common in insurance, business and law: *liability for* damages, *accept / deny liability*, *liability insurance*. The second sense is common in conversation and sports: *become a liability*, *a liability to / for* the team. In accounting, *liabilities* (plural) are debts, the opposite of *assets*.
entries.pattern: liability for something; accept / deny / limit liability; liability insurance; a liability to / for someone
examples: If a guest slips on your icy steps, you could face **liability** for their medical bills.
Our new goalkeeper is a **liability**; he's given up nine goals in two games.
The company denied any **liability** for the oil spill.

drill.sentence: In a small band, one member who's always late quickly becomes a {{liability}} for everyone else.
drill.hint: someone who causes trouble for the group (not *problem*, *burden* or *headache*)

entries.related: *responsibility* — more general; *burden* — something heavy to carry; *asset* — the opposite, a useful person or thing.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: Exactly and completely, with no exceptions; or in a way that must be obeyed.
entries.usage: Common in rules and signs: *strictly prohibited / forbidden / confidential*, *strictly enforced*. In the *exactly* sense it is common in speech: *strictly speaking*, *not strictly true*, *strictly between us*. *Strictly speaking* often introduces a small, technical correction.
entries.pattern: strictly prohibited / forbidden / confidential; strictly speaking; not strictly true / necessary
examples: Smoking is **strictly** prohibited anywhere on the hospital grounds.
**Strictly** speaking, a tomato is a fruit, not a vegetable.
Let's keep this conversation **strictly** between us, okay?

drill.sentence: This salary information is {{strictly}} confidential, so please don't share it with anyone.
drill.hint: with no exceptions at all (not *highly*, *completely* or *totally*)

entries.related: *precisely* — exactly; *rigidly* — without flexibility, often negative; *loosely* — the opposite (*loosely based on*).

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To weaken something important, such as safety, quality, security or integrity, or to put it at risk, often by accepting a lower standard.
entries.usage: Common in news, security, health and business: *compromise safety / quality / security / your integrity*, *a compromised immune system*, and in tech *the account was compromised* (hacked). It is often used in warnings or with *without* (*without compromising quality*). This is different from the everyday sense, reaching an agreement where both sides give something up.
entries.pattern: compromise safety / quality / security / integrity; be compromised; without compromising something
examples: The bakery cut costs without **compromising** the quality of its bread.
People with a **compromised** immune system should avoid crowded places during flu season.
Change your password right away if you think your account has been **compromised**.

drill.sentence: Driving with a cracked windshield can {{compromise}} your safety, especially in a crash.
drill.hint: make less secure (not *risk*, *affect*, *endanger*, *jeopardize* or *threaten*)

entries.related: *undermine* — weaken gradually; *jeopardize* — put in danger; *compromise* (noun) — an agreement where both sides give something up.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Important, serious or useful; having real value or purpose rather than being shallow or only for show.
entries.usage: Very common in speech and writing: *a meaningful relationship / conversation / change / difference*, *meaningful work*. In business and news it often points out the lack of real action (*no meaningful progress*). *A meaningful look* is one that silently sends a message.
entries.pattern: a meaningful relationship / conversation / change / difference; meaningful work / progress
examples: After years of office jobs, she wanted more **meaningful** work, so she became a nurse.
Visiting my grandmother every Sunday became the most **meaningful** part of my week.
Five dollars a month doesn't sound like much, but together our donations make a **meaningful** difference.

drill.sentence: Small talk is fine, but I'd rather have one {{meaningful}} conversation than ten polite ones.
drill.hint: having real depth and value (not *deep*, *real*, *serious* or *honest*)

entries.related: *significant* — large or important, often about numbers; *worthwhile* — worth the effort; *meaningless* — the opposite.

mistake.wrong: It's meaningful to book the hotel early in summer.
mistake.right: It makes sense to book the hotel early in summer.
mistake.why: German *sinnvoll* often means *sensible* or *a good idea*; English *meaningful* means important or deeply valuable.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The act of supplying something people need, such as care, services or housing; or a condition or part of a law, contract or agreement.
entries.usage: Formal and common in law, government and business: *the provision of* health care or services, *a provision in* the contract or law, *make provision(s) for* the future. In everyday talk people say *supply* or *a clause*; *provisions* (plural) can also mean food and supplies for a trip. German *Provision* (a sales fee) is *commission* in English.
entries.pattern: the provision of services / care; a provision in a law / contract; make provision for something
examples: The county is responsible for the **provision** of clean water to rural homes.
A **provision** in our lease says we can't have pets over twenty pounds.
A **provision** in the new state law lets restaurants serve food on the sidewalk until eleven at night.

drill.sentence: Before we signed, our lawyer pointed out a {{provision}} in the contract that let the seller cancel at any time.
drill.hint: part that sets out a rule (not *clause*, *condition*, *term* or *loophole*)

entries.related: *clause* — a numbered section of a legal document; *supply* — the everyday word for providing; *stipulation* — formal, a condition that is required.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To start again, or continue doing something, after a pause or interruption.
entries.usage: Common in news, announcements and work: *resume work / talks / service / play*, *resume + -ing*, *service will resume on Monday*. It is more formal than *start again* or *pick up where you left off*. Do not confuse it with *résumé* (REZ-uh-may), the American word for a CV.
entries.pattern: resume work / play / talks / service; resume + -ing
examples: The game **resumed** after a forty-minute rain delay.
Train service between the two cities will **resume** on Monday after the repairs.
After the baby was born, she **resumed** working part-time from home.

drill.sentence: We paused the movie for pizza and {{resumed}} it as soon as the delivery guy left.
drill.hint: started again from where we stopped (not *continued*, *restarted* or *unpaused*)

mistake.wrong: Please send your resume (rih-ZOOM) by Friday.
mistake.right: Please send your résumé (REZ-uh-may) by Friday.
mistake.why: The verb *resume* (rih-ZOOM) means start again; the document is a *résumé* (REZ-uh-may), often written without accents.

entries.related: *continue* — go on without stopping; *restart* — start again from the beginning; *pick up* — informal, continue.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To strongly advise or try to persuade someone to do something, often because it is important or urgent.
entries.usage: Common in news, official statements and serious advice: *urge someone to + verb*, *strongly urge*, *urge caution*, as in *officials urged residents to stay indoors*. It is stronger than *advise* or *encourage* but weaker than *order*. As a noun, *an urge* is a sudden strong wish (*the urge to eat chocolate*).
entries.pattern: urge someone to + verb; strongly urge; urge caution / patience
examples: Officials **urged** residents to stay off the roads until the ice melted.
My doctor **urged** me to cut back on salt.
Friends **urged** her to apply for the job, even though she didn't feel ready.

drill.sentence: Lifeguards are {{urging}} swimmers to stay out of the water because of strong currents.
drill.hint: strongly pressing (not *warning*, *asking*, *telling*, *encouraging* or *advising*)

entries.related: *encourage* — gentler; *advise* — give advice, neutral; *implore* — formal, beg desperately.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A part or share of a whole, often seen as a fraction or percentage; also, the correct relationship in size or amount between parts.
entries.usage: The first sense is common in news and reports: *a large / small / growing proportion of* people, *the proportion of* students who pass. The second appears in *in proportion to*, *out of proportion*, and *blow something out of proportion* (exaggerate it). It is more formal than *part* or *share*.
entries.pattern: a large / small proportion of something; in proportion to; out of proportion; blow something out of proportion
examples: A large **proportion** of our grocery budget goes to snacks for the kids.
Tips usually go up in **proportion** to the size of the bill.
You're blowing a tiny mistake out of **proportion**; nobody even noticed.

drill.sentence: Getting fired for being five minutes late? That punishment is completely out of {{proportion}} to the mistake.
drill.hint: the right balance in size or seriousness

entries.related: *percentage* — a part given as a number out of 100; *ratio* — the relationship between two amounts; *portion* — a part, often of food.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: Completely, carefully and in every detail; also used to mean *very much* before some verbs and adjectives.
entries.usage: Common with verbs of checking and cleaning: *thoroughly clean / check / research / test*, *wash thoroughly*. It also strengthens feelings and qualities: *thoroughly enjoy*, *thoroughly disappointed*, *thoroughly modern*. It is a little more formal than *really carefully* or *completely*.
entries.pattern: thoroughly clean / check / wash / research; thoroughly enjoy; thoroughly + adjective
examples: Wash the vegetables **thoroughly** before you cut them.
We **thoroughly** enjoyed our stay; the hosts made us feel at home.
Before you sign, read the contract **thoroughly**, especially the fine print.

drill.sentence: The mechanic {{thoroughly}} inspected the brakes before saying the car was safe to drive.
drill.hint: in full detail, missing nothing (not *carefully*, *fully* or *completely*)

mistake.wrong: Check the form throughly before you send it.
mistake.right: Check the form thoroughly before you send it.
mistake.why: The word is *thorough* + *-ly* (two syllables in *thorough*); *throughly* is a common misspelling.

entries.related: *carefully* — with attention, but not necessarily complete; *completely* — fully; *meticulously* — with great care over small details.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Unfriendly and aggressive toward someone, or strongly opposed to an idea or plan.
entries.usage: Common in news, work and conversation: *hostile to / toward* someone or an idea, *a hostile reaction / crowd / environment*, *a hostile takeover* (a company bought against its wishes). In US employment law, *a hostile work environment* means harassment serious or frequent enough to be illegal. Most Americans say HAHS-tul; HAHS-tyl is also heard in the US and is the usual British form.
entries.pattern: hostile to / toward someone or something; a hostile reaction / crowd / environment; a hostile takeover
examples: The new neighbors turned **hostile** as soon as we complained about their barking dog.
The board was **hostile** to the plan at first but approved it after a few changes.
The desert is a **hostile** environment for anyone without water or shade.

drill.sentence: The interview started politely, but the host became openly {{hostile}} when the singer refused to talk about her ex.
drill.hint: showing open dislike and anger (not *aggressive*, *rude*, *angry* or *combative*)

entries.related: *unfriendly* — milder; *antagonistic* — actively opposing; *welcoming* — the opposite; *hostility* — the noun.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Something you must do because of a law, a promise, a contract or a moral duty.
entries.usage: Common in law, business and everyday talk: *have an obligation to + verb*, *a legal / moral obligation*, *meet your obligations*, *out of obligation*. Ads promise *a free quote with no obligation*, meaning you don't have to buy. Americans also say *feel obligated to* for social pressure (*I felt obligated to invite him*), where British English prefers *obliged*.
entries.pattern: an obligation to + verb; a legal / moral / contractual obligation; meet your obligations; under no obligation
examples: Landlords have a legal **obligation** to keep apartments safe and heated.
I went to the reunion out of **obligation**, but I actually had a great time.
Call today for a free estimate with no **obligation** to buy.

drill.sentence: You're under no {{obligation}} to tip if the service was terrible, but most people still leave something.
drill.hint: binding duty (not *pressure* or *requirement*)

entries.related: *duty* — moral or job-related; *commitment* — a promise or responsibility you have accepted; *requirement* — something needed or demanded.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The amount by which spending is greater than income, or by which something is less than it should be.
entries.usage: Common in economics, news and sports: *a budget / trade deficit*, *run a deficit*, *cut / reduce the deficit*, and in sports *come back from a ten-point deficit*. It is also used for a lack of something: *a sleep deficit*. A deficit is the gap in one period; *debt* is the total amount owed over time.
entries.pattern: a budget / trade deficit; run / cut / reduce a deficit; come back from a ten-point deficit
examples: The city is facing a $20 million budget **deficit** and may have to close two libraries.
The team came back from a fifteen-point **deficit** to win in the last minute.
After a week of late nights, I've got a serious sleep **deficit**.

drill.sentence: Our chess club spends more on tournaments than it collects in fees, so it runs a {{deficit}} every year.
drill.hint: gap where spending is bigger than income (not *loss*)

entries.related: *debt* — the total amount owed over time; *shortfall* — an amount less than what is needed; *surplus* — the opposite.
